_source.displaydescription:
During special occasions such as jātrā and other festivities, the residents of Sunaguthi are supposed to worship four religious sites in the Sunaguthi area. This Mahākāla shrine is one of those four sites. On such occasions, long lines of devotees stand and queue in front of the shrine.

The shrine contains a statue of Mahākāla (38 × 27 cm) and is located inside the south-facing shikhara-style temple. Mahākāla is standing on top of a corpse and holding kartikā, kapāla and khaṭvāṅga. A square stone pillar with a lotus pedestal on top of it stands to the west of the structure. This pillar was erected in 1951 (VS 2008) by Guru Kavi Prasada after he organised the saptāha bhajana in Sunaguthi. Next to it, a wooden post supports a small bell bearing an inscription from VS 2031 (1974 CE). A copper plate inscription can be found on the western wall of the shrine and states that the statue was restored in 2001 CE (VS 2058).
_source.displayname: Mahākāla Shrine (ca. early 20th cent. CE) || महाकाल मन्दिर || SUN0200

_source.displaydescription:
Mati Bāhācā is a small courtyard containing two small monuments: one is a small shrine with Buddha’s image, and the other is a pañcāvaliyukta caitya. There is another courtyard is on the route leading from Naka Bahī to Dhalāyacā; one can cross through this to reach the Mati Bāhācā courtyard. This courtyard is not in fact a bahāḥ. Rather, it derives its name from Mati Bahā, and the fact that it is small in size. In 1863 CE (NS 983), Govinda Siṃha and his wife Vidyā Lakṣmī established a pañcāvaliyukta caitya inside the courtyard in memory of their son Jitamāna. After this, the courtyard began to be known as Govindasiṃha Vihāra. Local inhabitants also call this place Cibhāḥ Cuka.

A pancāvaliyukta caitya typically has five layers, consisting of images of lotuses, water, jewels, vajra and fire, and this one does not deviate from this structure. On the top of these layers (āvalis) is the sanctum (garbha) of the Caitya. Below this garbha one can find images of Buddha at each of the four cardinal directions. Five small images of Lakhinarasiṃha, Jitamāna, Matiju, Govindasiṃha and Vidyā Thakuṃ have been engraved on the Caitya’s western plinth. There is an oil-lamp balustrade surrounding the Caitya, which spans over the RCC beams. These in turn are supported by short pillars.

To the south of the Caitya is a small shrine made of stone with an image of Akṣobhya Buddha in its niche facing north. This shrine has been constructed on a plinth measuring 70 cm high and with a solid brick core. The Buddha image is housed in a smaller arched niche, also made of brick, which is covered by the stone slab roof of the stone temple. The stone temple structure itself measures 35 cm x 80 cm. The overall size of the temple is 150 cm x 120 cm, and it is 220 cm high. Its two-layered stone roof is decorated with lotus petals and crowned by a single ãvaḥsāḥ stone gajū. This in turn is backed by a brick masonry wall with a width equal to that of the stone temple. To the north of this shrine is a pañcāvali caitya constructed on a plinth measuring 150 cm high on a square base of 116 cm. There is also a newly established shrine for Sarasvatī near this shrine.

This courtyard is accessible from Mati Bāhā (to the west) through a narrow opening demarcated by two carved columns that are 120 cm in height. This route is open during matayāḥ and other such festivals.
_source.displayname: Mati Bāhācā (1863 CE) || मति बाहाचा || LAL0891

_source.displaydescription:
Vachẽ Nani Bāhāḥcā, a branch of Hakha Bāhāḥ (LAL0390), is located behind the Haka Bāhāḥ and on the eastern side of a narrow street that goes from the Haka Bāhāḥ to Ikhālakhu. The bāhāḥcā is a small courtyard (7.2 m x 7.2 m) and can be accessed through another courtyard which is attached to the street.

There is no kvaḥpāḥchẽ in this bāhāḥ. The main temple of the bāhāḥcā is built against the wall of a residential building facing west, and stands on a double plinth with a stone threshold. Timber lattice work surrounds the sanctum on three sides, whilst its rear wall is shared with the residential building. Inside, a statue of Akṣobhya has been placed on a high plinth so that it faces west. The roof is a two-tiered cement structure with a stone stūpa as its finial. A śikharakūṭotpannaparipadma caitya (187 cm high) can be found in front of the main temple structure at the centre of the courtyard. A statue of Gaṇeśa is located to the right of the temple and a statue of Hanumān can be found to its left. Both have been placed on the walls of the other buildings. 

This bāhāḥ was founded by Munirāja in 1909. The caitya was established prior to this in 1863, most likely by his father Dhanavantasiṃha Vajrācārya. This bāhāḥ is managed by three Vajrācārya families who are the descendants of Munirāja.
_source.displayname: Vachẽ Nani Bāhāḥcā (1909 CE) || वछेँ ननि बाहा:चा ।*। LAL0380

_source.displaydescription:
The single-storey Nārāyaṇa temple has a domed roof and is located on the eastern side of the road that runs north-south from Mangal Bazar to Lagankhel. The temple stands on a double plinth and can be accessed via stone steps to its west. The main arched entry is also to the west; blind stone doors can be found on the other three sides of the temple. There is a multi-layered terracotta motif above the entry level. A stone nāgo and floral (libī) motifl can be found almost half way up the temple, in between the layer and the base. All the doors are topped with kīrtimukha toraṇas.

A stone image of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu stands in the sanctum in a samapāda posture, holding śaṅkha and cakra in his two right hands, and gadā and padma in his left hands. Images of Lakṣmī and Garuḍa have been sculpted on the same stone. Lakṣmī stands to the left of Viṣṇu in tribhaṅga. Her left hand is shown performing a gesture of abhaya whilst her right hand performs varada. Garuḍa stands to Viṣṇu's right in samapāda, and is in a praying posture. Images of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu usually show Lakṣmī to his right and Garuḍa on his left. However, in this statue their position has been inverted. In addition to this main statue, there is also a smaller and partially damaged image of Viṣṇu in the sanctum. This has been placed inside a niche.

The rectangular base of the bell-shaped dome has a number of niches containing idols of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. These can be found on all four sides. A bronze pinnacle sits on top of the temple. Recently (in 2012), a wind vane was fixed next to the pinnacle, alongside statues of Viṣṇu's weapons. An oil-lamp balustrade with 108 lamps surrounds the temple, while a bell donated on the same date hangs on a beam besides the lower plinth at its southwest corner. A pillar with an image showing Garuḍa sitting and praying to Śrīdhara Viṣṇu was also erected in 2012.

No inscription mentioning the exact date of the establishment of the temple could be found. However, an astrologer called Śivanārāyaṇa installed a stone inscription dated NS 819 inside the temple. This stone records the names of his predecessors, and provides grounds to hypothesise that either he or one of them established the temple. Inside the sanctum, another broken inscription dated NS 754 informs readers of the renovation of a phalcā, which suggests that this inscription was brought here from somewhere else.  

The daily and annual ritual worships of this temple are no longer performed. The Cakravarti Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti organises the opening and closing of the temple.

_source.displaydescription:
Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ is one of the numerous small temples built in the Bāghabhairava Temple Complex (KIR0004). A Śivaliṅga is consecrated in the sanctum of this Degaḥ, and there is also one other Śivaliṅga in the sanctum.

There is no evidence to date the initial construction of the temple. However, a careful study of its wooden elements suggests that the temple might have been built around seventeenth and eighteenth century.

A sketch of the temple drawn by Henry Ambrose Oldfield around 1855 CE shows it in ruins with both roofs damaged completely. It is probable that the temple suffered severe damages during the 1832 CE earthquakes and was not renovated till 1850s. In the same sketch, a toraṇa can be seen crowning the temples's western door, which it does not exist in the present-day.

In the Rāṇā Period, the temple was reconstructed with a domed roof. It was dismantled and reconstructed as a tiered temple again in 1999 CE (VS 2056) (local knowledge, a local resident, Maharjana, male, age 53).

An inscription from 1844 CE (NS 964) is installed on the southern wall of the temple. It mentions that a phalcā was constructed around the place of Yamaleśvara, and reminds the members of the guṭhī about their obligations and duties. The phalcā is not related to the temple. On the basis of this inscription, Ś. Śreṣṭha (VS 2057, 44) named this temple as Yamaleśvara Mandira.

There is no guthi associated with Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ. Even elders of the local community cannot recall any guṭhī or any social or religious activities associated with the temple. A group of local youth lights up a bonfire on the day of Śivarātrī in front of the temple.
_source.displayname: Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ (built around seventeenth and eighteenth century) || महाद्य: देग: ll KIR0066

Naḥ Bāhāḥcā is one of the branches of Si Bāhāḥ (LAL0690) and is located at the south-west corner of the largest courtyard of Naḥ Bāhāḥ Nani. One can reach the bāhāḥcā via a narrow underpass from the south-west corner of the nani.

The two-storey building faces east, and an aṣṭakoṇoparipadma caitya stands in front of its sanctum. The principal façade of the monument building has a carved wooden door at its centre flanked by two small lattice windows. There is no toraṇa but small images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara surmounted by a small caitya image have been fixed to the lintel above the door. Two small niches made from wooden frames also flank the sanctum entrance. Stone statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla have been placed in the niches to the left and right respectively. The front wall of the first storey has been separated into three sections. One part contains the sanctum door, one part has a Gaṇeśa statue and the third part holds a Bhairava statue. The joint line between these sections is clearly visible. A band of carved wooden cornice separates the first floor from the second floor. The façade of the first floor largely consists of an intricately carved three bay window (pasukājhyāḥ) which is flanked by two small blind windows. The remaining wall area has been painted white. Figures of Namasaṅgīti and Amoghapāśa are displayed on either side of the window, whilst images of the Seven Buddhas can be seen above the window. The roof of the god house is made from corrugated metal sheets and supported by plain struts. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined inside the sanctum.

The literal meaning of Naḥ Bāhāḥ is ‘a new monastic building’. Recently, the monastic building located at the north-east corner of this small monastic building was known as Naḥ Bāhāḥ. However, locals claim that this Naḥ Bāhāḥcā (LAL0530) is the original Naḥ Bāhāḥ. In earlier times, a pond called Khāsāpukhū was located to the north west of this bāhāḥcā. However, the pond has since been filled in and a school named Svatantra Śikṣā Sadana runs this area. The bāhāḥcā was given its classical name, Yokulivarṇa Mahāvihāra, due to its proximity to the pond; yokuli means 'north-western direction' in the Nevārī language.

No sources could be found with which to date the initial construction of this bāhāḥcā. Pruscha 1975 (1975, C/P-53) dates this monument to the 17th century and mentions that it was renovated by a guṭhī in 1933, though he does not provide evidence to support this claim. A palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 688 (1548 CE) makes mention of a monastic building named Naka Bāhāra. It could be that this refers to the present monument. Long ago, most of the saṅgha members of the bāhāḥcā were Śākyas who were carpenters by occupation. Locke (1985: 178) mentions that the last surviving male member of this household died without any sons. Afterwards, the husbands of his daughters inherited the rights, duties and properties of their father-in-law. Later, these families stopped performing social and religious activities in the bāhāḥcā. At present, four families affiliated with the Āagama Guṭhī of the Naḥ Bāhāḥ Nani perform daily ritual worships in the bāhāḥcā. When cuḍākaraṇa (shaving one's hair for the first time), initiations, jaṃko and other rituals are organised in the Si Bāhāḥ, these people also come to visit this bāhāḥcā.
_source.displayname: Naḥ Bāhāḥcā (before 1548 CE) || नः बाहाःचा || LAL0530

_source.displaydescription: The two-storey Sataḥ faces towards the east. No historical record is available to date the building. Villagers from Tamang and Magar communities would stay overnight in this Sataḥ when they came to the Valley to sell their local products, though this no longer seems to be the case. Ekatā Paṭhaśālā was established in the building during the Rana period. Afterwards, the building was used by the Ganesh Youth Club, and the first floor of the building was also used by the Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti. The office was moved to a new building constructed on top of the filled in pond to the north of Tāpā Hiti Phalcā East (LAL4199). This likely occured some time in the 2010s. At present, the ground floor of the Sataḥ is used to store old materials. The sataḥ building has been deteriorating over time and was further damaged by the earthquakes of 2015. The inner walls of the building have cracked in many places.
_source.displayname: Tāpā Hiti Sataḥ || तापा हिति सत: || LAL4201

The office was moved to a new building constructed on top of the filled in pond to the north of Tāpā Hiti Phalcā East (LAL4199). This likely occured some time in the 2010s. At present, the ground floor of the Sataḥ is used to store old materials. The sataḥ building has been deteriorating over time and was further damaged by the earthquakes of 2015. The inner walls of the building have cracked in many places.

_source.displaydescription:
The Buramāṃ Vaidya Bāhāḥ is a branch of Cikã Bahī (LAL1620) and lies to its north. The courtyard is surrounded by residential housing and can be entered through the gates of a private house.

The dyaḥchẽ (god house) is located on the south of the courtyard with its sanctum on the ground floor. An oil-lamp balustrade is fixed on the plinth of the dyaḥchẽ. A torana above the entrance displays Buddha, Nāmasaṅgīti and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara. The sanctum's carved central door is flanked by plain lattice windows and small statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla have been placed in the ground floor wall niches. In the sanctum statues of Buddha, Nāmasaṅgīti and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara rest on stone pedestals. A statue of Mañjuśrī is enshrined inside a room to the right of the sanctum and a statue of Vasundharā resides in the room to the left of the sanctum. 

The houses on the west and north sides of the courtyard are built in traditional Newar style with colonnaded ground floors and carved triple-bay windows on their first and second floors. These openings have cusped arches and can be dated to the early Saha period. Both houses have two new additional floors on top. The house on the east has been completely rebuilt in modern style. According to a local resident, all of the houses were once owned by the same family and used to be interconnected, however, they were later divided among the brothers.

The surfaces of these houses are a particularly interesting feature of this courtyard. Each of the plastered surfaces of the walls facing into the courtyard has been decorated with wall paintings. The surfaces seem to have been made from a mixture of mud, rice husk and cow dung. Some of the wall paintings depict various deities, while others (such as the wall of the western corner of the god-house) are covered in verses in Sanskrit, most probably excerpts from the Jātaka tales (see photo: LAL1630_I_20191006_01). Most of the painted surfaces have eroded and only a few traces of the paintings remain intact today. A photo printed in Locke (1985, 213) shows that the house on the eastern side also had similar paintings and windows, however since its reconstruction it no longer has these features. On the wall paintings are depictions of various deities, some from Jātaka tales,

Locke (1985, 214) maintains that the Bāhāḥ was founded in NS 986 (1866 CE) without providing a source. A stone inscription on the vedi of the northern face of the dharmadhātu jinālaya caitya mentions that Maṇiratna Vaidya enshrined the images of Triratnas in the sanctum in NS 998. Three days afterwards, the naming ceremony of the monastic building took place, where it was given the name "Maṇikūṭa Vihāra". The families affiliated with the guṭhī of the monastic building were professional vaidyas (practitioners of Ayurvedic medicine); the monastic building is therefore also known as Vaidya Bāhāḥ.
